source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese Children's Riddles as a Benchmark for Machine Insight and Metacognition (NazoNazo)
finding: 38 LLMs were tested on riddles that need a representational shift. Humans beat nearly all models. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning ones.
numbers: 201 riddles; 120-item human subset. Humans about 52.9% accuracy (126 adults). Non-reasoning models mean 7.6% (n=16), reasoning models 17.6% (n=19). Mean over models 18.88%. Only GPT-5 reached human level. Zero-shot, temperature 0.
limits: Single group preprint; Japanese wordplay may not match matchstick-type restructuring; contamination possible for public items; no scaffold prompts tested.
agent_relevance: Plain zero-shot models are far below humans on insight items. A scaffold has real headroom, but the gap may be about verification, not generation (see c03).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese Children's Riddles as a Benchmark for Machine Insight and Metacognition (NazoNazo)
finding: Reasoning vs non-reasoning difference is large and model size does not matter. Scale alone does not buy insight.
numbers: Model-level: mean difference 9.80 percentage points, 95% CI [3.0,16.6], Cohen d=0.946. Pooled logistic over 201 items: odds ratio 2.29 (CI 1.99-2.64). Item-level accuracy 9.42% vs 19.25%. Parameter size vs accuracy Pearson r=-0.017; release date Spearman 0.402 (p=.0123, n=38).
limits: Observational comparison across vendors; reasoning label is confounded with release date.
agent_relevance: Spending more thinking tokens helps, parameter count does not. Trigger design should be about use of thinking budget, not a bigger model.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese Children's Riddles as a Benchmark for Machine Insight and Metacognition (NazoNazo)
finding: Verification failure: models often produced the correct answer as a candidate in their thought log and then rejected it or chose another. Humans rarely do this.
numbers: Examples in Grok-4 (Q18, Q26, Q31, Q198) and Claude-opus-4 (Q35, Q135, Q179, Q183). Reported as informal candidate tracking, no rate given.
quote: Wait! I've got it! "Parking"! A parking lot! No, that still doesn't connect
limits: Qualitative; no counted percentage; authors call it hypothesis-generating.
agent_relevance: Key for triggers: after a restructure is proposed, the agent needs a code-checked acceptance test (G2/G3). Do not let the model re-judge its own candidate by feel.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese Children's Riddles as a Benchmark for Machine Insight and Metacognition (NazoNazo)
finding: Models show feeling-like talk (feels forced, dead end, brilliant) that seems to help drop or keep candidates. A weak feeling of rightness is the proposed bottleneck.
numbers: Overall accuracy: Grok-4 37.6%, Claude-opus-4 30.3%, DeepSeek-R1-0528 22.9%, Gemini-2.5-flash-preview 10.9%. Gemini returned to an earlier point ('I'm back to...') 29 times.
limits: Anecdotal log reading by the authors; self-reported feelings of an LLM are not shown to be causal.
agent_relevance: Supports an external impasse and acceptance signal built from counts and checks, not model self-reports.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese Children's Riddles as a Benchmark for Machine Insight and Metacognition (NazoNazo)
finding: Thinking language did not help: reasoning in Japanese was not more accurate than in English.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 thought in Japanese in 100% of logs. Gemini-2.5-flash: 6.0% Japanese, 0% accuracy there vs 11.7% English. Claude-opus-4: Japanese 36.7% vs English 28.7% (not significant). Grok-4: Japanese 29.5% vs English 48.8%.
limits: Small per-language cells for some models.
agent_relevance: Language of reasoning is not the lever for restructuring; reframing needs a different mechanism.

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks: benchmark for visual symbolic compositional reasoning with matchstick puzzles
finding: Matchstick-equation puzzles (the Knoblich paradigm) are hard for strong vision-language models and easy for humans.
numbers: 14 VLMs. Humans average 91.72% (3 adults, about one minute each). Best model o3: 60.00% with text prompt, 38.50% pure visual, 49.25% mean over both. Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25% text, 22.50% visual. Gemini-2.5-Flash 26.50% text, 8.50% visual.
limits: Human sample is 3 people; tasks are generated and include visual parsing, which mixes restructuring with perception. 82% of items need two-stick moves.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that matchstick restructuring is not solved by plain frontier models, even in text. A good test bed for trigger choice.

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks: benchmark for visual symbolic compositional reasoning with matchstick puzzles
finding: Difficulty rises with number of moves and operator changes; reasoning models beat their base models.
numbers: o3 text-prompted: 73% on the easiest level, 55-56% on harder levels. Reasoning vs base: o3 60.00% vs GPT-4o 0.00%; Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25% vs Flash 26.50%; Seed-1.6-Thinking 21.50% vs its base 3.25%.
limits: Accuracy only; no analysis of which restructuring type (constraint relaxation vs chunk decomposition) fails.
agent_relevance: Chunk-type difficulty is not separated here. A run that tags items by Knoblich type (loose vs tight chunk) would fill the gap.

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks: benchmark for visual symbolic compositional reasoning with matchstick puzzles
finding: Giving the equation as text removes a perception cost and lifts every model, so some failure is parsing, not restructuring.
numbers: o3 38.50% without text vs 60.00% with text. Gemini-2.5-Pro one-move puzzles: 51.7% text vs 25.8% pure visual.
limits: Large synthetic set (1.4M instances), curated test set only.
agent_relevance: When using matchstick-style tasks for the agent, supply the symbolic form so the test measures restructuring.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) Leveraging Speech to Identify Signatures of Insight and Transfer in Problem Solving
finding: Human think-aloud on five matchstick-arithmetic problems; GPT-5.1 labelled each utterance with one of seven reasoning-move labels. Same-type sequences gave transfer.
numbers: N=189 participants, 945 trials, 47.5% correct (449/945). Value-loose-chunk easiest 80.7%, tautological hardest 19.2%. Same condition accuracy 0.32 on trial 1 to 0.75 on trial 5; Different stayed 0.32-0.39 (trial x group beta=-0.524, p<.001).
limits: Human study; LLM only an annotator; annotation noise; first success is a proxy for restructuring; 4-minute limit.
agent_relevance: The Knoblich difficulty order (loose chunk easy, tight chunk and tautology hard) still holds, and an LLM annotator can extract a speech marker of restructuring.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) Leveraging Speech to Identify Signatures of Insight and Transfer in Problem Solving
finding: At first success people consider fewer distinct candidate moves, and in the Same group they narrow further afterwards. Search narrows when structure is found.
numbers: Distinct candidate moves at first success vs before: Same beta=-2.11 (95% CI -2.97,-1.18); Different -2.24 (CI -3.07,-1.41). Post-success vs first success: Same -0.58 (CI -1.06,-0.13); Different +0.05 (CI -0.65,0.77).
limits: Speech is an incomplete window on cognition (authors).
agent_relevance: A measurable agent signal: distinct candidates falling after a successful reframe. Could drive a reuse-the-discovered-operator step.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset and the Einstellung effect
finding: LLMs show fixation-like failure: puzzles with red herrings are much harder than the same puzzles with red herrings removed.
numbers: On original walls GPT-4 solved only single-digit numbers of 494 walls (humans 285/494 walls, 1405/1976 groups). On red-herring-diluted OCW-Randomized GPT-4 solved up to about 68 walls; on OCW-WordNet (no red herrings) up to 471. Best few-shot connection F1 about 41-45% vs human about 80%.
limits: Table rows in the PDF text were jumbled, so the per-row mapping is approximate; GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 only; no reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Red herring strength predicts failure, as the human fixation account says. A scaffold should suppress the strongest-association candidates on a signal, not on a schedule.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset and the Einstellung effect
finding: Few-shot examples gave gradual gains but did not fix fixation. GPT-4 improved with more shots.
numbers: GPT-4 improves monotonically with 0, 1, 3, 5, 10 shots, with small steps; still far below human on the original walls. Misformatted outputs 4.4%, hallucinated clues 6.6%.
limits: In-context learning only; exact per-shot numbers not extracted cleanly.
agent_relevance: Prompt examples alone are not a restructuring mechanism.

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: a caution against anthropocentrism
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on insight problems that have a short path through questioning an assumption. Models did better here than on analytic problems.
numbers: 5 insight problems. GPT-3.5 got 1.5 to 3.5 of 5 across four runs; GPT-4 got 4.5 of 5 in one run. Humans solved each problem 44-61%. GPT-3.5 per-problem rates 25-75%. Correlation of human vs GPT-3.5 per-problem rate r=-0.63 (four observations). Analytic problems: 0 correct for both models.
limits: Tiny sample; partial credit for the non-insight route; contamination unclear.
agent_relevance: Item difficulty for the model does not track human difficulty, so human trigger data cannot be copied one-to-one onto an LLM.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT matched the most likely human score on 30 verbal insight problems.
numbers: 30 problems (15 practice, 15 transfer), human rates from 20 subjects. Pooled ChatGPT score 12 of 30; practice 7/15, transfer 5/15. No difference between sets (Fisher p<0.72). Score pattern within the top 5% of human outcome probabilities.
limits: Small human sample (20); the claim that ChatGPT can be trained in out-of-the-box thinking is not backed by a training manipulation; problems may be on the web.
agent_relevance: Early GPT-3.5-class result. Verbal insight items are no longer a reliable discriminator.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Lateral-thinking multiple-choice puzzles. The best model (ChatGPT) sat about halfway between chance and humans. Reconstruction variants expose memorisation.
numbers: Random 25%; ChatGPT 53% (word puzzles) and 63% (sentence puzzles); humans 91.67% (3 experts, 102 items). About a third of models at or below random. Instruction-tuned models improve with scale.
limits: Multiple choice; humans only 102 items; later work reports near-ceiling with prompting (c16).
agent_relevance: Semantic and context reconstructions show models can win by memory; an insight test for the agent needs perturbed variants (matches G3).

source: Mizumoto et al. 2025 citing Bai et al. 2025 (AAAI) metacognitive prompting on BRAINTEASER
finding: Secondhand: metacognitive prompting (MP) is said to push GPT-4 above 98% on BRAINTEASER, past human level. I could not open the AAAI paper (access denied).
numbers: GPT-4 with MP above 98% accuracy (as cited by the NazoNazo authors); human 91.67% in BRAINTEASER.
limits: Secondhand number; the MP paper itself was not opened; saturation means BRAINTEASER cannot separate scaffolds.
agent_relevance: A prompt scaffold can close the gap on easy lateral items. It was not tested on harder restructuring tasks.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Spontaneous mid-trace Aha shifts are rare, do not become more frequent with RL training, and go with lower accuracy.
numbers: 1M+ traces, hundreds of GRPO checkpoints (Qwen2.5 and Llama), 3 domains (math, crosswords, Rush Hour). Shifts in about 6.31% of traces; accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for non-shifted. Formal Aha detector fired on only 1.79% of samples.
limits: Cue detection uses words like 'wait'; may miss unlexicalised restructuring (authors); small base models; Rush Hour accuracy near 0%.
agent_relevance: Do not count on the model restructuring by itself. G1 (doubt only on a signal) is supported: spontaneous doubt is noise.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Forced reconsideration works when gated by uncertainty. A second pass with an appended reconsideration cue raised math accuracy.
numbers: Paired samples: Math p(Pass1)=0.3221 to p(Pass2)=0.4062, +8.41 points (50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong; N=320,000). Crosswords +0.45 points (5,380 vs 5,004). Rush Hour +0.01. Gains larger in the top-20% entropy bucket.
quote: artificially triggering extrinsic shifts under high entropy reliably improves accuracy
limits: Gain depends on domain; entropy needs token probabilities; no gain when base rate is near zero.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for an entropy-gated reframe trigger: code reads entropy and fires one reconsideration pass. Fits G1 and the program-decides rule.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: In math, spontaneous shifts hurt even in the high-entropy stratum, and hurt most in the low-entropy majority.
numbers: Raw accuracy difference shifted minus non-shifted: Math high entropy -7.40 points, low entropy -22.88 points; Xwords high entropy +0.63 points (coefficient p=0.904). Shift-entropy link pooled OR 0.77, p=0.070, N=723,200; positive in Xwords (OR 2.05) and RHour (1.19), negative in Math (0.58).
limits: Entropy is a sequence-level mean; domain differences are large.
agent_relevance: The model cannot be trusted to know when to rethink; the program should choose. Trigger by entropy or failed check, not by in-text 'wait'.

source: Guo et al. (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing reasoning capability via reinforcement learning
finding: Source of the aha-moment claim: RL-trained R1-Zero shows a rise in reflective words such as 'wait' and a mid-trace change of approach.
numbers: AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during RL training without SFT. 'Wait' use shows spikes after step 8000.
quote: That's an aha moment I can flag here.
limits: Shown as one example and a word-frequency curve; no test that the shifts caused the gains (see c17-c19 follow-up).
agent_relevance: Gives a training-time route to reflection. Our agent works through a scaffold with no training, so only the idea of a reconsideration cue transfers.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two alternative theories of insight (JEP:LMC 29(5))
finding: Target paper of this subfield: representational change vs progress monitoring in an unlimited-move task. Not opened by this agent; see angle A and B files for numbers.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: No LLM has been tested head to head on the two theories; our agent can only test them as trigger rules (impasse detector vs progress monitor).

source: Latif et al. (2024) cited as evidence that SOTA models may surpass humans on candle, nine-dot and RAT
finding: Cited by Mizumoto et al. as saying models already beat humans on classic insight tasks. I could not find or open the Latif paper; the claim is secondhand.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Secondhand; search APIs were rate limited.
agent_relevance: Classic textbook insight items are probably contaminated; use new or generated items.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Origin of the two mechanisms (constraint relaxation, chunk decomposition) used by the matchstick LLM work above. Seen only as a search snippet.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Gives an item taxonomy for building LLM tests.

source: Graf et al. (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis
finding: Eye tracking on matchstick problems; only nonlinear models detected the abrupt representational change. Snippet only.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: A change-point method could be run on an agent's candidate trace to detect restructuring.

source: Search note: no study found that tests LLMs on a Jones-2003 style head-to-head theory comparison
finding: Across 6 web searches and 8 opened PDFs or pages, no paper tests representational change vs progress monitoring in an LLM. Closest are MathSticks, NazoNazo and Illusion of Insight.
numbers: Zero direct tests found.
limits: arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate limited, so recall is limited.
agent_relevance: The comparison for our agent must be our own experiment: an impasse-triggered reframe vs a progress-monitor-triggered reframe on generated matchstick items.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese Children's Riddles as a Benchmark for Machine Insight and Metacognition (NazoNazo) - search-capable models
finding: Three retrieval-augmented models were run as a contamination probe; the main endpoint is retrieval-free.
numbers: Search models n=3 (Gemini-2.0-Flash, 4o-mini-search-preview, GPT-4o-search-preview).
limits: Retrieval-arm results were not recorded in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is not the stated cause of the gap.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models - comparison with our G1 data
finding: Their result agrees with our own: forced doubt on a schedule is not the point; gated doubt is. Raw spontaneous shifts correlate with failure.
numbers: Our schema note: word puzzles 92% plain vs 75% with forced doubt (our measurement, not theirs).
limits: Different tasks; theirs is a cue-appended second pass, ours is forced doubt in-stream.
agent_relevance: Combine: no schedule; gate on entropy or a failed check; one second pass only.
